data.description: The original clinical use of rapamycin (as sirolimus), preventing organ rejection by suppressing T cell activation. It is no longer standard first-line maintenance; today it is used in selected regimens, often to spare calcineurin inhibitors.

page_status.reason: By design: fewer than three linked studies and not a node on the pathway map, so no page is generated. The record is still served here and in the bulk exports.

data.description_beginner: The original medical use of rapamycin: preventing the immune system from rejecting a transplanted organ by suppressing T-cell activation. It is not the standard first choice today, but it is still used in selected patients, often to cut down the dose of the harsher usual drugs.

studies.title: Rapamycin and human longevity among kidney transplant recipients surviving the first year.

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human (US national organ transplant registry: 4,885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin vs 6,589 not prescribed; alive with functioning graft at 1 year; median follow-up 11 years)
studies.finding: In a US registry cohort of 11,474 kidney transplant recipients who were alive with a functioning graft at one year, 4,885 were prescribed rapamycin and 6,589 were not; 6,443 died during a median follow-up of 11 years. After propensity-score weighting for age, BMI, diabetes and 15 other factors, median survival age was 64.6 years with rapamycin and 64.3 years without (95% CI for the difference -1.6 to 2.0 years), so no meaningful survival benefit was seen. Boundary: observational registry data in transplant recipients who are also on other immunosuppressants and who entered the cohort only by having survived twelve months after transplant, rapamycin given at immunosuppressive doses by clinician choice; it does not test low-dose or intermittent rapamycin in healthy older adults.
